claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a pre-existing hierarchical heterostructure with distinct phase boundaries.
The hierarchical heterostructure contains internal stresses.
In-situ neutron diffraction can continuously monitor diffraction-peak shifts and broadening during room-temperature tensile deformation.
Peak-position shifts and peak broadening can be calibrated to the onset of plasticity and fracture.
Local lattice distortion and internal-stress evolution occur at phase boundaries during deformation.
Changes in diffraction-peak characteristics capture real-time microstructural alterations under tensile stress.
The diffraction-detected microstructural alterations precede yielding and fracture.
Correlating diffraction features with macroscopic deformation events can be used to infer mechanical properties.
The diffraction-based model can predict Young's modulus.
The diffraction-based model can predict yield strength.
The diffraction-based model can predict fracture onset.
The model is expected to improve predictive accuracy for yield strength and fracture initiation by approximately 15–25% relative to established full-scale simulations.
The model is expected to reduce prediction time by roughly an order of magnitude relative to established full-scale simulations.
Established full-scale simulations require extensive computational time.
Established full-scale simulations may fail to capture rapid structural transitions.
The approach may fail when neutron-diffraction signals are dominated by noise or measurement artifacts.
The approach may fail when calibration does not capture the complexity of the diffraction features.
The method may not generalize beyond the tested temperature and loading conditions.
A prediction error greater than ±10% for yield strength or fracture onset across multiple runs would falsify the hypothesis.
